blocks.text: חָרְכָה. מִתְּמִימֵי פְּרָכָה. וְנִתַּן לָהּ אֲרֻכָה: רָחֲבָה וְאָרְכָה. וְקֶשֶׁת דָּרְכָה. וְעֹל הֶאֱרִיכָה: בִּעֲתָה בְּרַכָּה. וְהִנֵּה דְּרוּכָה. וְעַד עַתָּה מוֹלְכָה: יְסוֹדוֹת עֵרְמָה. עֵרָה וְהֶחֱרִימָה. וְעַד יְסוֹד עָרְמָה: רֹאשׁ הֵרִימָה. וְסוֹד הֶעֱרִימָה. וְיָדֶיהָ רָמָה: בָּעֲרָה מֵעָרְמָה. וְעַד שַׁחַק רוֹמָה. וְתֶאְפּוֹד מְלוּכָה: יְרִיעוֹתַי גִּדְדָה. אֳהָלַי שִׁדְּדָה. וְחָרְשָׁה וְשִׂדְּדָה: קְצִינוּת רָפְדָה. וּמַלְכוּת אָפְדָה. וְזֹאת הִקְפִּידָה: יָזְמָה וּמָרְדָה. עֲבוֹד
uncertainties: The poem continues from the previous page and runs on to the next one (it ends mid-phrase with עֲבוֹד).
מִתְּמִימֵי: I can't tell the vowel under the first mem (hiriq or patah) or under the second-to-last mem (tsere or patah).
פְּרָכָה: I can't tell whether the mark under the pe is a sheva or a qamats.
אֲרֻכָה: I can't confirm the vowel under the resh (qubbuts?) or whether there is a dagesh in the kaf.
בִּעֲתָה: I can't tell whether the bet has a hiriq or a sheva.
וְעַד (line 3) and וְעַד (lines 4–5): there is a mark near the vav/ayin that could be a patah (וַעַד) or a meteg. I can't resolve it.
עֵרְמָה (line 3): there is a mark at the right edge before the ayin, possibly a meteg. I can't tell whether the resh has a sheva or a qamats (עֵרָמָה).
עָרְמָה (line 4) and מֵעָרְמָה: I read the resh as having a sheva, but I'm not certain.
גִּדְדָה: I can't tell whether the gimel has a hiriq or a tsere, or whether the first dalet has a dagesh.
אֳהָלַי: the alef pointing (hataf qamats, qamats or holam) is unclear.

The rubric is in small Rashi type. The facing English page reads 'On Sabbath.' I can't tell whether the first word is חזן or something like בְּ/לְ. Check this against a higher-resolution image.

blocks.text: אֶדֶר וָהוֹד אֶתֵּן בִּצְבְיוֹן. שֶׁוַע אֶעֱרוֹךְ בְּנִיב וְהִגָּיוֹן.

blocks.text: Morning Prayer for the New Year

men and has achieved length of rule. It has expanded greatly, stretched the bow and extended far its yoke. It has frightened the tender people (Israel) and trampled it down, and rules to this day. It has loosened and destroyed the foundation stones of the Temple and laid them bare down to the ground. It has lifted up its head, devised a secret plan and stands there powerfully. It is ablaze with guile, raises itself up to heaven and girds itself in majesty. My tapestries has it torn, destroyed my tabernacles, ploughed and harrowed its site. It has acquired dominion, wrapped itself in might and offended this people (Israel). It initiated rebellion, served idols zealously
uncertainties: The source hyphenates 'ac-quired' across a line break. I joined it as 'acquired'.

blocks.text: Let the tribes of those Thou hast called, arise and rule, cut off the branches of enemies and let them fall, for both kingdom and ruler belong to the Lord, the Holy One.
May our exiled ascend from afar His holy mountain that we may praise Him always in His Inner Sanctuary, for He has remembered His holy word, the Holy One.
All inhabitants of the world and dwellers on earth do constantly say: Great things has the Lord performed on earth, and the Lord shall be King over all the earth, the Holy One.
uncertainties: There is a stray speck before 'world' ('·world'). It looks like a printing blemish, not punctuation, so I left it out.

blocks.text: Glorification and praise willingly do I bestow, I order prayer in speech and thought, I call upon the supreme God. On the day chosen from the mighty heavens for upright judgment to glorify His holiness, the Lord rules, the earth rejoices. The world is too small to contain His loftiness, who is there able to describe His might? King of all the earth is God, then sing with understanding.
uncertainties: After 'I order' there is a small speck that may be a dot. It is probably a blemish.
The first letter looks like resh, but it could be dalet. The Hebrew stanza begins דֵּעַ.

blocks.text: May all His creatures acquire perception and know how great is His might. A memorial has He established for His wonders. He has firmly planted His foundation stone (Torah), the divine gift, so as to rejoice in His people. He remembers His covenant for ever.

notes: I read both whole pages (s134 and s135), since the ignore-above-the-rule instruction applies only to s124/125. The text above the rule continues the poem from the previous page and runs on to the next page with עֲבוֹד.

Speaker sigla on s134: חו״ק (probably חזן וקהל, i.e. cantor and congregation) marks the first two Sabbath stanzas. Then ח׳ (cantor) and ק׳ (congregation) alternate within each alphabetic stanza: א, ב, ג, ד, ה.

Printed conditional alternative: in Metz, the stanza beginning כל יושבי תבל is not said. It is enclosed in parentheses with a Rashi-type rubric. The English page translates the stanza and has no equivalent of the Metz rubric.
The Hebrew refrain cue שְׁמוֹ מְפָאֲרִים after the gimel stanza does not appear on the English page. It stays absent from the English.
On the English page the Hebrew alphabetic stanzas are grouped as אדר (א–ג) and רע/דע (ד–ה). The 'the Holy One' endings correspond to the Hebrew קָדוֹשׁ: refrains.
There are no Biblical cantillation marks on either page. Small marks before some words (before ayin in עֲלוֹת, עֲבוּר, עֵרְמָה and others) may be meteg. Each one is flagged rather than asserted.
Proposed corrections for possible typos: the English linkage cue 'רע' should probably be 'דע' if the glyph is in fact resh. I propose no other corrections.

The image resolution limits how reliably I can read fine pointing in the top poem lines, the Rashi rubric חזן שבת(?) and the sigla. The uncertainties for each block list the specific marks that need a third reader.
